source.title: Detection of COVID-19 & non-COVID diseases from chest-X-rays using deep learning-based CNNs

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no obvious truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares optimizer and batch-size settings on chest-X-ray classification test accuracy, but does not test random-label memorization or measure training-to-test gaps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-set classification accuracies for selected model, optimizer, and batch-size combinations, and states that performance improved by 10–30% with variations in batch size and optimizer. These are results on natural disease labels, not arbitrary-label controls; training error and generalization gaps are not reported. The cited studies in its introduction and discussion are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The reported results do not establish whether any claim version holds. Optimizer and batch size were varied, but only selected configurations and an unspecified aggregate improvement are reported. Comparisons across different architectures cannot isolate optimizer effects, and no within-model small-versus-large batch outcome is recoverable. The large-batch generalization claim is cited as background.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' claim that optimizer and batch-size choices affect classification performance, including their unspecified 10–30% improvement statement. Their main conclusion is that a three-stage toolchain using selected pretrained CNN configurations achieves stage accuracies of 99%, 98%, and 97%. They acknowledge that broader independent validation is needed. They report no measured training-to-test gaps.
record.recipe_differences: Transfer learning on natural chest-X-ray disease labels; three pretrained CNNs, a fixed 10-epoch budget, and batch sizes 6, 8, and 10. No random-label task or train-test gap analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that classification performance changed with optimizer type and batch size; the reported best settings differ by stage.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report 10–30% improvements from varying optimizer and batch size, without identifying the baseline, specific conditions, metric, or direction of either factor's effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer and batch-size choices can affect pretrained CNN classification performance on chest X-rays.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected configurations achieve 99% accuracy with SqueezeNet/SGDM/batch 6, 98% with ResNet-50/RMSprop/batch 8, and 97% with EfficientNet-b0/Adam/batch 6 on three different classification tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different selected CNN configurations perform best at different stages of this chest-X-ray classification pipeline.

record.peer_reviewed: Soft Computing - A Fusion of Foundations, Methodologies and Applications
record.problems: The optimizer and batch-size comparisons are not reported as condition-specific test-accuracy results in the supplied text. The paper does not report training accuracy or loss alongside test performance, and the CovidApp validation uses only four independent images.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the text provides no separately recoverable outcome for each optimizer or batch-size condition. The stated 10–30% aggregate improvement does not identify a baseline, metric, or condition-specific value. Stage accuracies concern selected best models and do not isolate optimizer or batch-size effects.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

Adaptive versus SGDM held-out performance under comparable conditions; tuning-dependent changes, training performance, and optimizer remedies. Selected configurations use different architectures and sometimes different batch sizes.

Whether increasing batch size beyond a workload-dependent threshold worsens held-out performance at fixed epochs, and whether adapted recipes recover performance. Ten epochs are fixed, but outcomes for the batch-size sweep are not reported.
Held-out effects of adding or removing dropout, including interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with alternative generalization measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The absence of training performance alone would not prevent testing V4 or V5: comparable held-out outcomes could suffice. Here the decisive limitation is the absence of reported within-model optimizer or batch-size comparisons. The record's rows_left_out already declares these reporting limitations, so no missing-result entry is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels under the same training recipe.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error across widths.
Convolutional versus fully connected network comparison.

The paper varies optimizers and reports test accuracy, but does not report training performance or the training-to-test gap needed to assess whether adaptive optimizers generalize worse at equal or better training performance.

The paper varies batch size at a constant 10 epochs and reports an aggregate 10–30% improvement with hyperparameter variations, but does not give a condition-specific small-versus-large batch comparison or measure the generalization gap.
Dropout conditions and their effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 5.4 discusses excessive batch size affecting generalization and cites Keskar et al.; the reported results do not test that effect.

tranche.reason: Sections 5.4, 6 and 10 report hyperparameter tuning and selected CNN configurations, but no within-model comparisons establishing V4's optimizer disadvantage or V5's large-batch penalty. No other version is tested or used.

source_check.notes: The 10–30% improvement in section 10 has no specified baseline, metric, or direction for either hyperparameter. Selected configurations' stage accuracies cannot isolate optimizer or batch-size effects.
